## Question and background

## Data preparation and exploration

```{r}
# Data prepration
library(knitr)
df <- read.csv("data/ObesityDataSet_raw_and_data_sinthetic.csv")

# Transform categorical predictors into factors (including response)
# We won't need the response here, but it'll be useful in supervised learning
cat_cols <- c("Gender", "family_history_with_overweight", "FAVC", "CAEC",
              "SMOKE", "SCC", "CALC", "MTRANS", "NObeyesdad")
df[cat_cols] <- lapply(df[cat_cols], factor)

# Make CAEC, CALC, and NObeyesdad ordered
df$CAEC <- ordered(df$CAEC, 
                   levels = c("no", "Sometimes", "Frequently", "Always")
                   )
df$CALC <- ordered(df$CALC, 
                   levels = c("no", "Sometimes", "Frequently", "Always")
                   )
df$NObeyesdad <- ordered(
  df$NObeyesdad,
  levels = c("Insufficient_Weight", "Normal_Weight", 
             "Overweight_Level_I", "Overweight_Level_II", 
             "Obesity_Type_I", "Obesity_Type_II","Obesity_Type_III")
  )

X <- df[, -ncol(df)] # removes last column of df (response)

# Exploration
# boxplots of numerical variables
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
boxplot(df$Age,
        main = "Age Distribution",
        ylab = "Age",
        col = "deepskyblue")

boxplot(df$Height,
        main = "Height Distribution",
        ylab = "Height",
        col = "darkorange")

boxplot(df$Weight,
        main = "Weight Distribution",
        ylab = "Weight",
        col = "indianred1")

# Obesity level distribution
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 9, 4, 2))
obesity_counts <- table(df$NObeyesdad)
barplot(obesity_counts,
        horiz = TRUE,
        las = 1,
        main = "Obesity Level Distribution",
        xlab = "Count",
        ylab = "",
        col = hcl.colors(length(obesity_counts), palette = "Pastel 1")
        )

# Age vs. Obesity Level
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
boxplot(Age ~ NObeyesdad, data = df, 
        horizontal = TRUE,
        las = 1,
        main = "Age by Obesity Level",
        xlab = "Age",
        ylab = "",
        col = hcl.colors(length(obesity_counts), palette = "Pastel 1")
)

# Height vs. Obesity Level
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
boxplot(Height ~ NObeyesdad, data = df, 
        horizontal = TRUE,
        las = 1,
        main = "Height by Obesity Level",
        xlab = "Height",
        ylab = "",
        col = hcl.colors(length(obesity_counts), palette = "Pastel 1")
)

# Weight vs. Obesity Level
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
boxplot(Weight ~ NObeyesdad, data = df, 
        horizontal = TRUE,
        las = 1,
        main = "Weight by Obesity Level",
        xlab = "Weight",
        ylab = "",
        col = hcl.colors(length(obesity_counts), palette = "Pastel 1")
        )
```

## Unsupervised Learning

### Hierarchical Clustering

```{r}
library(cluster)
gower_distance <- daisy(X, metric = "gower")

h_cluster <- hclust(gower_distance, method = "complete")
h_cluster2 <- hclust(gower_distance, method = "single")
h_cluster3 <- hclust(gower_distance, method = "average")

# Complete linkage
plot(h_cluster, labels = FALSE,
     main = "Complete Hierarchical Clustering of Obesity Data",
     xlab = "Individuals",
     ylab = "Gower Distance")

# Single linkage
plot(h_cluster2, labels = FALSE,
     main = "Single Hierarchical Clustering of Obesity Data",
     xlab = "Individuals",
     ylab = "Gower Distance")

# Average linkage
plot(h_cluster3, labels = FALSE,
     main = "Average Hierarchical Clustering of Obesity Data",
     xlab = "Individuals",
     ylab = "Gower Distance")

# Compare numbers of clusters from average linkage
cluster2 <- cutree(h_cluster3, k = 2)
cluster3 <- cutree(h_cluster3, k = 3)
cluster4 <- cutree(h_cluster3, k = 4)
cluster5 <- cutree(h_cluster3, k = 5)
cluster10 <- cutree(h_cluster3, k = 10)
cluster15 <- cutree(h_cluster3, k = 15)
cluster20 <- cutree(h_cluster3, k = 20)

table(cluster2)
table(cluster3)
table(cluster4)
table(cluster5)
table(cluster10)
table(cluster15)
table(cluster20)

# Find lengths
length3 <- silhouette(cluster3, gower_distance)
length4 <- silhouette(cluster4, gower_distance)
length5 <- silhouette(cluster5, gower_distance)

# Compare averages of silouhette widths
avg_sil3 <- mean(length3[,3])
avg_sil4 <- mean(length4[,3])
avg_sil5 <- mean(length5[,3])

# Results for k = 3, 4, and 5
data.frame(
  k = c(3, 4, 5),
  avg_silhouette = c(avg_sil3, avg_sil4, avg_sil4)
)
```

### Spectral Clustering

For a dataset that consists of continuous and categorical predictors, Gower distance was used for spectral clustering. Gower distance measures how similar two observations are when there is a mixed dataset (Source: <https://crispinagar.github.io/blogs/gower-distance.html>).

```{r}
library(SpectralClMixed)
library(GGally)
set.seed(42301)

# Find the best number of cluster (k)
k_vals <- seq(from = 2, to = 10, by = 1)
gower_dist <- daisy(X, metric = "gower")

# Initialize
spectral.fits <- vector("list", length(k_vals))
comparison <- data.frame(
  k = k_vals,
  avg_silhouette = NA_real_,
  category_wt = NA_real_,
  bt_wt_ss = NA_real_,
  smallest_cluster = NA_integer_
)
cluster_cols <- paste("Cluster", seq_len(max(k_vals)))
comparison[cluster_cols] <- 0L

for (i in seq_along(k_vals)){
  k <- k_vals[i]
  
  # Perform spectral clustering on mixed dataset (categorical + numeric)
  spectral.fits[[i]] <- mspec(X, k = k, starts = 10, its = 100)
  
  cluster_sizes <- table(factor(spectral.fits[[i]]$cluster, levels = seq_len(k)))
  silhouette_value <- silhouette(spectral.fits[[i]]$cluster, gower_distance)
  
  comparison$avg_silhouette[i] <- mean(silhouette_value[, "sil_width"])
  comparison$category_wt[i] <- as.numeric(spectral.fits[[i]]$"cat_wt")
  comparison$bt_wt_ss[i] <- as.numeric(spectral.fits[[i]]$"bt/wt_ss")
  comparison$smallest_cluster[i] <- min(cluster_sizes)
  comparison[i, paste0("Cluster ", seq_len(k))] <- as.integer(cluster_sizes)
}

comparison

# Parallel-coordinate plot for k = 2
cols <- 1:16
parallel_data <- X[, cols, drop = FALSE] # copies columns from X

# Convert factors to numeric codes for plotting only
parallel_data[] <- lapply(parallel_data, function(x){
  if (is.factor(x)) as.numeric(x) else x
})

spectral.fit_k2 <- spectral.fits[[which(k_vals == 2)]]
parallel_data$Cluster <- factor(spectral.fit_k2$cluster) # adds fitted cluster assignment for each observation

ggparcoord(
  data = parallel_data,

)

# Parallel-coordinate plot for k = 3

```

When increasing `k`, it is difficult to tell if there are distinguished clusters because the lines overlap a lot in the parallel-coordinate plots. $k = 2$ has the highest average silhouette of about 0.077. An average silhouette score near 0 indicates that the observations are close to the boundaries of their cluster and another cluster or that clusters are overlapping, which can be observed from the parallel-coordinate plots (Source: <https://machinelearningmastery.com/k-means-cluster-evaluation-with-silhouette-analysis/>). From $k = 3$ to $k = 10$, the average silhouette values are either negative or close to 0. Negative average silhouette scores suggest that the observations are closer to another cluster than their assigned cluster, on average.

As $k$ increases, the bt_wt_ss value (ratio of between-cluster sum of squares to within-cluster sum of squares) decreases. $k = 2$ has the highest bt_wt_ss value, which would indicate that the clusters are farther apart from one another compared to the observations within their assigned cluster. However, the very low average silhouette score means there is weak separation.

Overall, $k = 2$ may seem like the best number of clusters, but the evidence is weak. None of the $k$ values had strong evidence of separated clusters.

## Supervised Learning

### KNN

```{r}
library(kknn)
library(caret)
set.seed(43201)

# Change NObeyesdad to an unordered factor b/c we only care about classifying exact labels
df$NObeyesdad <- factor(
  df$NObeyesdad, 
  levels = levels(df$NObeyesdad), 
  ordered = FALSE
  )

# Perform a 80/20 data split
train_rows <- createDataPartition(y = df$NObeyesdad, p = 0.80, list = FALSE)
train_data <- df[train_rows, ]
test_data  <- df[-train_rows, ]

# Tune parameter k (number of clusters)
# train.kknn() does NOT use Gower's distance and uses leave-one-out CV
# Manhattan distance
knn.fit_manhattan <- train.kknn(
  NObeyesdad ~ ., 
  data = train_data,
  ks = seq(from = 1, to = 20, by = 1),
  distance = 1, # Manhattan distance
  kernel = c("rectangular", "triangular", "epanechnikov", 
             "biweight", "triweight", "gaussian", "optimal"),
  scale = TRUE)

summary(knn.fit_manhattan)

# Euclidean distance
knn.fit_euclidean <- train.kknn(
  NObeyesdad ~ ., 
  data = train_data,
  ks = seq(from = 1, to = 20, by = 1),
  distance = 2, # Euclidean distance
  kernel = c("rectangular", "triangular", "epanechnikov", 
             "biweight", "triweight", "gaussian", "optimal"),
  scale = TRUE)

summary(knn.fit_euclidean)

# Choose best model and evaluate it
knn.fit_best <- knn.fit_manhattan
test_pred <- predict(knn.fit_best, newdata = test_data)
test_cm <- confusionMatrix(data = test_pred, reference = test_data$NObeyesdad)

test_cm
test_cv <- 1 - test_cm$overall["Accuracy"] # test misclassification rate
test_cv
```

KNN was tested with Manhattan distance and Euclidean distance. The kernel type and $k$ were tuned wit leave-one-out cross-validation. KNN with Manhattan distance has a misclassification rate of 0.106, triangular as its best kernel, and $k = 7$ as its best number of clusters. KNN with Euclidean distance has a misclassification rate of about 0.156, biweight as its best kernel, and $k = 15$ as its best number of clusters. Based on the misclassification rate alone, it appears that the KNN with Manhattan distance is better due to its lower misclassification rate.

KNN with Euclidean distance also has a larger number of clusters. "Larger neighborhoods average more noise, making the fitted function more stable. They also reach farther from the target, which can hide local features of the sine curve. Smaller neighborhoods retain those features but are more sensitive to the noise." (Source: <https://teazrq.github.io/stat432rpy/topics/nearest-neighbors/knn-and-local-averaging.html>).

The best settings for `knn.fit_manhattan` were used on a testing dataset. Its misclassification rate is `r round(test_cv, digits = 4)`. This is a fairly low test error, which suggests that the candidate model can make good predictions.

### Random Forest

## Analysis Skill

### Goal and data

We classify the seven-level `NObeyesdad` outcome from the other 16 predictors in the [UCI obesity dataset](https://doi.org/10.24432/C5H31Z). The 2,111 records have no missing values; class counts range from 272 to 351. Nominal predictors are dummy-coded; ordered `CAEC` and `CALC` use ordered-factor contrasts. A linear kernel tests a straight boundary in the encoded predictors; polynomial and radial kernels allow nonlinear boundaries. UCI reports that 77% of records were synthetically generated, so strong performance may not generalize to independently collected populations.

### Tuning and selection

With seed 43201, reserve a stratified 20% test set, used only once after model selection. Compare 15 settings with the same stratified five folds on the remaining data: linear, polynomial (degrees 2 and 3), and radial kernels. Tune cost `C`, which penalizes margin violations; for radial kernels also tune `gamma`, which controls boundary locality. Polynomial `gamma = 1/p` and `coef0 = 1`, where `p` is the encoded predictor count. Within each fold, center and scale encoded predictors using that fold's training data only. Select the setting with the lowest mean cross-validation misclassification rate and compare it with a majority-class baseline.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-dpi: 130
library(e1071)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

data_file <- if (file.exists(file.path("data", "ObesityDataSet_raw_and_data_sinthetic.csv"))) {
  file.path("data", "ObesityDataSet_raw_and_data_sinthetic.csv")
} else {
  file.path("project", "data", "ObesityDataSet_raw_and_data_sinthetic.csv")
}
df <- read.csv(data_file, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

class_levels <- c(
  "Insufficient_Weight", "Normal_Weight", "Overweight_Level_I",
  "Overweight_Level_II", "Obesity_Type_I", "Obesity_Type_II",
  "Obesity_Type_III"
)
df$NObeyesdad <- factor(df$NObeyesdad, levels = class_levels)
stopifnot(!anyNA(df))

nominal <- c(
  "Gender", "family_history_with_overweight", "FAVC",
  "SMOKE", "SCC", "MTRANS"
)
df[nominal] <- lapply(df[nominal], factor)
df$CAEC <- ordered(df$CAEC, levels = c("no", "Sometimes", "Frequently", "Always"))
df$CALC <- ordered(df$CALC, levels = c("no", "Sometimes", "Frequently", "Always"))

y <- df$NObeyesdad
predictor_data <- df[, setdiff(names(df), "NObeyesdad"), drop = FALSE]
X <- model.matrix(~ ., data = predictor_data)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
p <- ncol(X)

set.seed(43201)
test_index <- unlist(lapply(class_levels, function(cl) {
  rows <- which(y == cl)
  sample(rows, size = floor(0.2 * length(rows)))
}), use.names = FALSE)
train_index <- setdiff(seq_along(y), test_index)

fold_id <- integer(length(train_index))
y_train <- y[train_index]
for (cl in class_levels) {
  rows <- which(y_train == cl)
  fold_id[rows] <- sample(rep(seq_len(5), length.out = length(rows)))
}

grid <- rbind(
  data.frame(kernel = "linear", degree = NA_integer_,
             cost = c(0.1, 1, 10), gamma = NA_real_),
  expand.grid(kernel = "polynomial", degree = 2:3,
              cost = c(0.1, 1, 10), gamma = NA_real_),
  expand.grid(kernel = "radial", degree = NA_integer_,
              cost = c(0.1, 1, 10), gamma = c(0.5 / p, 1 / p))
)
grid$cv_error <- NA_real_
fold_errors <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = 5, ncol = nrow(grid))
fold_baseline_errors <- numeric(5)

standardize_from <- function(train, other) {
  center <- colMeans(train)
  spread <- apply(train, 2, sd)
  spread[!is.finite(spread) | spread == 0] <- 1
  list(
    train = sweep(sweep(train, 2, center, "-"), 2, spread, "/"),
    other = sweep(sweep(other, 2, center, "-"), 2, spread, "/")
  )
}

fit_candidate <- function(x, response, setting) {
  args <- list(
    x = x, y = droplevels(response),
    kernel = as.character(setting$kernel),
    cost = setting$cost, scale = FALSE
  )
  if (setting$kernel == "polynomial") {
    args$degree <- setting$degree
    args$gamma <- 1 / p
    args$coef0 <- 1
  }
  if (setting$kernel == "radial") args$gamma <- setting$gamma
  do.call(e1071::svm, args)
}

for (fold in seq_len(5)) {
  fold_train <- train_index[fold_id != fold]
  fold_valid <- train_index[fold_id == fold]
  majority_class <- names(which.max(table(y[fold_train])))
  fold_baseline_errors[fold] <- mean(y[fold_valid] != majority_class)
  transformed <- standardize_from(X[fold_train, , drop = FALSE],
                                  X[fold_valid, , drop = FALSE])
  
  for (j in seq_len(nrow(grid))) {
    fit <- fit_candidate(transformed$train, y[fold_train], grid[j, ])
    pred <- predict(fit, transformed$other)
    fold_errors[fold, j] <- mean(pred != y[fold_valid])
  }
}

grid$cv_error <- colMeans(fold_errors)
baseline_cv_error <- mean(fold_baseline_errors)
grid$selected <- ""
best_index <- which.min(grid$cv_error)
grid$selected[best_index] <- "Yes"

candidate_label <- function(row) {
  kernel <- switch(as.character(row$kernel),
                   linear = "Linear",
                   polynomial = paste0("Poly-", row$degree),
                   radial = paste0("RBF \u03b3=", signif(row$gamma, 2))
  )
  paste0(kernel, ", C=", row$cost)
}
grid$candidate <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
  candidate_label(grid[i, ])
}, character(1))

plot_data <- grid
plot_data$candidate <- factor(
  plot_data$candidate,
  levels = plot_data$candidate[order(plot_data$cv_error, decreasing = TRUE)]
)
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = candidate, y = cv_error, color = kernel)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_point(
    data = plot_data[best_index, , drop = FALSE],
    shape = 8, size = 4, color = "firebrick"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "Mean 5-fold CV misclassification",
    color = "Kernel",
    caption = "The red star marks the lowest-error setting selected for final testing."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8.5),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8.5)
  )
```

```{r}
report_grid <- data.frame(
  Model = grid$candidate,
  `CV error` = sprintf("%.3f", grid$cv_error),
  Selected = grid$selected,
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(report_grid, align = c("l", "r", "c"))
```

**Selected setting:** `r grid$candidate[best_index]` (mean CV error `r sprintf("%.3f", grid$cv_error[best_index])`). The majority-class baseline has mean CV error `r sprintf("%.3f", baseline_cv_error)`.

### Held-out evaluation

Refit the selected setting on the complete training set, then evaluate once on the reserved test set. The table reports one-vs-rest counts for each class; because this is a seven-class task, TN/FP/FN/TP are class-specific.

```{r}
final_transform <- standardize_from(
  X[train_index, , drop = FALSE],
  X[test_index, , drop = FALSE]
)
final_fit <- fit_candidate(final_transform$train, y[train_index],
                           grid[best_index, ])
test_pred <- factor(
  predict(final_fit, final_transform$other),
  levels = class_levels
)
test_truth <- factor(y[test_index], levels = class_levels)
test_majority_class <- names(which.max(table(y[train_index])))
baseline_test_accuracy <- mean(test_truth == test_majority_class)
confusion <- table(Actual = test_truth, Predicted = test_pred)

tp <- diag(confusion)
fn <- rowSums(confusion) - tp
fp <- colSums(confusion) - tp
tn <- sum(confusion) - tp - fn - fp
ovr <- data.frame(Class = class_levels, TN = tn, FP = fp, FN = fn, TP = tp)
rownames(ovr) <- NULL

test_accuracy <- mean(test_pred == test_truth)
macro_recall <- mean(tp / (tp + fn))

kable(ovr, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

The selected model's held-out accuracy is **`r sprintf("%.3f", test_accuracy)`** (`r sum(test_pred != test_truth)` errors among `r length(test_truth)` cases), versus **`r sprintf("%.3f", baseline_test_accuracy)`** for the majority-class baseline; macro-averaged sensitivity is **`r sprintf("%.3f", macro_recall)`**. The one-vs-rest counts show which categories are confused. These results estimate performance on one stratified split, not independently collected populations; the dataset is predominantly synthetic, and weight/height are closely associated with obesity class.
